name: FC-51 IR obstacle avoidance sensor
description: Reflective infrared obstacle detector: an IR LED and IR receiver face forward, and an LM393 comparator turns the reflected light into a digital output that goes LOW when an object is within the range set by the potentiometer (about 2-30 cm, 35 degree cone). Open-collector output with a 10 kOhm pull-up to VCC on the board. Runs on 3.3-5 V. Sold as: FC-51 IR obstacle avoidance sensor module (common blue 3-pin clone board: OUT, GND, VCC).
eli5: Shines invisible light forward and tells your board when something is close enough to bounce it back, like a robot's whisker.

pins.name: OUT
pins.description: Digital output: LOW when an obstacle is detected, HIGH (pulled up to VCC by 10 kOhm) when clear (pin 1)

pins.name: VCC
pins.description: Supply, 3.3-5 V (pin 3). With a 3.3 V board connect it to 3V3, because OUT is pulled up to VCC.

supplierQuery: FC-51 IR obstacle avoidance sensor module
buildNotes: Header order as printed: OUT, GND, VCC. It is not the usual VCC-first order, so check the labels before wiring.
On an ESP32 or Pico power VCC from 3V3: the board's 10 kOhm pull-up takes OUT to VCC, so a 5 V supply puts 5 V on the GPIO.
OUT is active LOW: it reads 0 when something is in front of the sensor and 1 when clear. The second LED on the board lights when it detects.
Turn the blue potentiometer to set the trigger distance (about 2-30 cm). Clockwise usually increases range; if the detect LED stays on with nothing in front, turn it back.
Black or dark matte objects reflect little IR and may not be seen; sunlight and incandescent light can cause false triggers.

example.code:
from fc51 import FC51
import time

sensor = FC51({OUT})
while True:
    print('Obstacle: %s' % ('YES' if sensor.obstacle() else 'no'))
    time.sleep(0.5)

test.title: Reports an obstacle when the sensor is triggered
